options: Seine-Saint-Denis, one of France's poorest suburbs
quiz.explanation: The Paris 2024 Olympic Athletes' Village was built in Seine-Saint-Denis, one of France's poorest suburbs, to be converted to housing and create lasting infrastructure legacy.

laws.title: Wine Appellation Reform and Climate Adaptation
laws.subtitle: AOC rules updated to allow new grape varieties
laws.fullDescription: France's INAO (Institut National de l'Origine et de la Qualité) approved landmark reforms allowing traditional wine appellations to incorporate new grape varieties better suited to warming climates. Bordeaux can now blend in heat-tolerant varieties, while Champagne approved seven new grape types. The reform balances preserving heritage with adapting to climate change threatening iconic French wine regions.
laws.penalty: Producers using unauthorized varieties lose appellation status and premium pricing
exceptions: Experimental plots under research exemption
Vin de France category allows broader variety use

laws.title: Political Fragmentation and Hung Parliament Crisis
laws.subtitle: France operates with no stable majority after snap elections
laws.fullDescription: President Macron's snap election gamble in June 2024 backfired, producing a hung parliament with no stable majority. Three blocs — left (NFP), centrist (Macron's alliance), and right (RN) — are roughly equal. Michel Barnier became prime minister but was quickly removed by a no-confidence vote. France faces governance paralysis with a rising debt-to-GDP ratio and inability to pass budgets. Le Pen's RN party continues to rise. France holds the EU's rotating presidency while unable to govern domestically.
laws.penalty: Caretaker government has limited constitutional powers, unable to pass controversial legislation
exceptions: Presidential prerogatives in defense and foreign policy continue unaffected by parliamentary deadlock
Emergency legislation can be passed through Article 49.3 executive procedure

laws.title: Airbus Dominance and European Aviation Strategy
laws.subtitle: France co-leads Europe's aviation champion against Boeing
laws.fullDescription: Airbus, headquartered in Toulouse, France, has surpassed Boeing as the world's largest commercial aircraft manufacturer by deliveries. France is the largest single Airbus stakeholder nation. The A320neo family dominates narrowbody orders. Airbus is developing hydrogen-powered aircraft (ZEROe) for potential 2035 entry. French aerospace cluster around Toulouse (Safran, Thales, Dassault) employs hundreds of thousands. The EU's aviation industrial strategy is central to French economic policy.
laws.penalty: Aircraft manufacturers must meet EASA certification standards; safety violations face production halts
exceptions: Defense aircraft production follows separate procurement and certification rules
Research and experimental aircraft have lighter requirements than commercial certification

quiz.q: When did Airbus surpass Boeing as the world's largest commercial aircraft manufacturer?
quiz.explanation: Airbus definitively surpassed Boeing in deliveries following Boeing's 737 MAX crisis, which grounded the aircraft for 20 months after two crashes — Airbus has maintained its lead since 2019.

laws.title: Tourism Giant and Cultural Heritage Economy
laws.subtitle: France remains world's most visited country with 100 million tourists
laws.fullDescription: France is the world's most visited country with nearly 100 million tourists annually. Paris — the Eiffel Tower, Louvre, Versailles — draws visitors globally. France earns €65+ billion from tourism. The 2024 Paris Olympics attracted record attention. Beyond Paris, wine regions (Bordeaux, Burgundy, Champagne), châteaux, and the French Riviera draw discerning tourists. France's cultural heritage (UNESCO World Heritage Sites) is a diplomatic and economic asset managed by the Culture Ministry.
laws.penalty: Historic monuments and heritage sites have strict modification restrictions protecting their character
exceptions: Temporary event structures in heritage areas require special permits but are allowed
Film and photography productions in iconic sites require authorization and location fees

quiz.q: How many tourists visit France annually?
quiz.explanation: France receives nearly 100 million tourists annually — more than any other country in the world — with Paris alone attracting tens of millions, making tourism a central pillar of the French economy.

laws.title: Pension Reform Protests and Fifth Republic Legitimacy
laws.subtitle: France's social contract under strain from austerity measures
laws.fullDescription: French President Emmanuel Macron's decision to use Article 49.3 of the constitution to bypass parliamentary vote on pension reform in 2023 — raising the retirement age from 62 to 64 — sparked massive protests and a constitutional crisis of legitimacy. The reform itself was contested by a majority of the French public, and the use of executive power to circumvent parliament inflamed opposition across the political spectrum. France experienced months of strikes and demonstrations, with over a million people marching repeatedly. The Constitutional Council validated the reform but the political damage was significant. France's social model — featuring generous pension benefits, strong labor protections, and shorter working hours than other developed nations — is under structural pressure from demographic change (fewer workers per retiree) and fiscal sustainability concerns. The 2024 snap elections following the European Parliament vote produced a hung parliament, further complicating governance. France's Fifth Republic constitutional structure, designed by de Gaulle to give the executive strong powers, faces legitimacy questions when those powers are used against clear popular opposition.
laws.penalty: No direct penalties for the pension reform; labor law violations can carry fines and back-payment requirements
exceptions: Some public sector workers retain different pension schemes with earlier retirement provisions

quiz.q: What constitutional mechanism did Macron use to pass pension reform without a parliamentary vote?
quiz.explanation: Macron used Article 49.3 of the French constitution, which allows the executive to bypass a parliamentary vote and pass legislation directly, though it risks a no-confidence motion — a highly controversial use that sparked widespread protests.

laws.title: Nuclear Energy Renaissance and European Power Export
laws.subtitle: France reaffirming nuclear power as its strategic energy advantage
laws.fullDescription: France generates approximately 70% of its electricity from nuclear power — the highest proportion of any country — giving it among Europe's lowest-carbon and lowest-cost electricity. After years of planned nuclear phase-down under the Hollande government, President Macron reversed course, announcing plans to build six new EPR2 reactors and potentially eight more, while extending the operational life of existing reactors. France sees nuclear energy as both a strategic energy security asset and a climate solution. France is a leading exporter of electricity to neighboring European countries, particularly during shortages. EDF (formerly fully state-owned) manages France's nuclear fleet. However, major maintenance issues reduced French nuclear output in 2022 significantly. France is also developing offshore wind and solar while maintaining nuclear as the backbone. The EU's taxonomy debate over whether nuclear qualifies as sustainable investment was partly won by France, with nuclear included.
laws.penalty: Nuclear plant operators face strict regulatory requirements from ASN (Nuclear Safety Authority); violations carry significant penalties
exceptions: Military nuclear activities operate under separate defense frameworks

quiz.q: Approximately what percentage of France's electricity comes from nuclear power?
quiz.explanation: France generates approximately 70% of its electricity from nuclear power — the highest proportion of any country — giving it among Europe's lowest-carbon electricity grids and making it a net electricity exporter to neighboring countries.

laws.title: Political Fragmentation and Cohabitation
laws.subtitle: Macron's snap election gamble creates ungovernable assembly
laws.fullDescription: President Macron's surprise dissolution of parliament in June 2024 backfired dramatically. The resulting election produced a hung parliament with three roughly equal blocs: left-wing NFP, centrist Ensemble and right-wing RN, none with majority. France entered a period of political instability with multiple prime ministers in 2024-2025. The government struggled to pass budgets and faced constant censure threats, while Macron remained as president until 2027 with diminished authority.
laws.penalty: Government can use Article 49.3 to pass budget without vote but triggers censure motion risk
exceptions: President retains exclusive authority over foreign policy and defense
Emergency powers under Article 16 available in extreme national crisis

quiz.q: What triggered France's 2024 political crisis?
quiz.explanation: President Macron's surprise dissolution of parliament in June 2024 triggered snap elections that produced a hung parliament and profound political instability.

laws.title: Pension and Budget Crisis Austerity
laws.subtitle: France struggles to reduce deficit under political paralysis
laws.fullDescription: France faces significant fiscal pressure with a deficit running well above EU limits at over 6% of GDP. The hung parliament makes budget passage extremely difficult, with multiple no-confidence motion threats. Prime Minister Michel Barnier was ousted in a no-confidence vote in December 2024 after just three months, the shortest French government in modern history, when his budget was rejected. France's debt levels and deficit trajectory have attracted bond market attention, raising France's borrowing costs.
laws.penalty: EU excessive deficit procedure activated for France; budget must reduce deficit below 3% GDP within defined timeframe
exceptions: France retains national fiscal sovereignty within EU treaty constraints
Emergency borrowing during economic crises exempt from some restrictions

quiz.q: How long did French Prime Minister Michel Barnier's government last before being ousted by a no-confidence vote?
quiz.explanation: Michel Barnier's government lasted just three months—the shortest French government in modern history—before being ousted by a no-confidence vote in December 2024 when parliament rejected his budget.

laws.title: Mistral AI and European AI Sovereignty
laws.subtitle: French startup challenges US AI dominance with open models
laws.fullDescription: Mistral AI, a Paris-based startup founded by former DeepMind and Meta researchers, raised billions in funding and released competitive large language models that challenged US AI dominance. Mistral's open-source approach—releasing model weights publicly—differed from OpenAI's closed approach and attracted significant developer adoption. The company became a European champion for AI sovereignty, with French government support and EU interest in maintaining competitive AI capability. Mistral's success validated the European AI ecosystem's ability to compete with Silicon Valley.
laws.penalty: AI models deployed commercially must comply with EU AI Act transparency requirements
exceptions: Open-source model releases have reduced but not eliminated EU AI Act obligations
Research versions have different compliance timeline than commercial releases

quiz.q: What approach did Mistral AI take to its language models that differed from OpenAI?
options: Open-source model releases with publicly available weights
quiz.explanation: Mistral AI took an open-source approach to its language models, releasing model weights publicly—in contrast to OpenAI's closed approach—which attracted significant developer adoption and established Mistral as a European champion for AI sovereignty.

laws.title: Nuclear Renaissance and New Reactor Program
laws.subtitle: France doubles down on nuclear as others hesitate
laws.fullDescription: France generates about 70% of its electricity from nuclear power—the highest share globally—and has doubled down on nuclear energy as a cornerstone of its decarbonization strategy. President Macron announced plans for 14 new EPR2 reactors while extending the life of existing plants. France's reliance on nuclear power insulates it from gas price volatility and provides low-carbon electricity. However the existing fleet has suffered from significant maintenance problems and new reactor construction has faced delays and cost overruns at Flamanville.
laws.penalty: Nuclear power plants require ASN (Nuclear Safety Authority) licensing; each reactor extension requires safety assessment approval
exceptions: Research reactors at universities have different regulatory pathway
Fusion research projects operate under different framework than commercial fission

quiz.q: What percentage of France's electricity comes from nuclear power?
quiz.explanation: France generates about 70% of its electricity from nuclear power—the highest share of any country globally—and has doubled down on the technology by planning 14 new reactors while extending existing plant lifetimes.

laws.title: Climate and Resilience Law
laws.subtitle: Citizens' Convention Becomes Law
laws.fullDescription: France's 2021 Climate and Resilience Law emerged from the Citizens' Convention on Climate, a deliberative democracy experiment where 150 randomly selected citizens developed climate proposals. The law introduces dozens of measures: banning short domestic flights where a train journey under 2.5 hours exists, ending advertising for fossil fuels, labeling products with carbon footprints, renovating energy-inefficient buildings (making them illegal to rent by 2028), and creating a ecocide crime. France committed to 40% emissions reduction by 2030 and carbon neutrality by 2050.
laws.penalty: Landlords renting energy class G buildings after 2025 face fines; ecocide: up to 10 years imprisonment and €4.5 million fines
exceptions: Island and remote communities for short-haul flight bans
Heritage buildings exempt from some renovation requirements

laws.title: French Universal Healthcare (Assurance Maladie)
laws.subtitle: Best Healthcare in the World?
laws.fullDescription: France's Assurance Maladie provides near-universal health coverage, consistently ranked among the world's best healthcare systems by WHO. France's system reimburses patients 70-100% of costs, with complementary private insurance ('mutuelle') covering most remaining costs — with 95% of French people having a mutuelle. France allows patients to choose any doctor, specialist, or hospital. France pioneered the carte vitale — a health chip card — for seamless claim processing. The system has high satisfaction rates but faces financial pressures from aging, and France has been reforming to emphasize prevention.
laws.penalty: Employers must contribute 13.1% of wages; failure to enroll is illegal; fines for non-compliance
exceptions: EU citizens receive coverage in France
Undocumented immigrants covered by AME (emergency medical aid)

laws.title: French 35-Hour Workweek and Labor Code
laws.subtitle: Le Code du Travail
laws.fullDescription: France's 35-hour workweek, implemented in 2000 under Prime Minister Jospin, made France the first major economy to institutionalize shorter working hours as a job-sharing strategy. While actual hours worked often exceed 35, overtime premiums apply. France's Code du Travail is one of the world's most comprehensive labor codes — over 3,500 pages. French workers have among the strongest protections globally: mandatory 5 weeks' paid vacation, strong redundancy protections, and extensive union rights. France's 2023 pension reform — raising the retirement age from 62 to 64 — triggered the largest wave of strikes in decades.
laws.penalty: Labor code violations: DRT (Labor Inspectorate) fines and prosecution; unauthorized dismissal: industrial tribunal compensation
exceptions: Executive and management positions exempt from 35-hour rule
Agreements may allow longer hours with compensatory rest

laws.title: French Grandes Écoles and Republican Education
laws.subtitle: Grandes Écoles vs. Universities
laws.fullDescription: France has a unique two-tier higher education system: public universities (open admission, low fees ~€500/year) and elite Grandes Écoles (Sciences Po, ENA/INSP, École Polytechnique, HEC) which admit through highly competitive concours exams and produce France's top officials and executives. France provides free education from preschool (école maternelle from age 3) through university. France's 1905 laïcité (secularism) law prohibits religious symbols in public schools — headscarves banned since 2004, abayas banned since 2023. The baccalauréat (national exam at 18) determines university access.
laws.penalty: School attendance mandatory from 3 to 16; religious symbol violations: suspension; private school registration required
exceptions: Religious schools (enseignement catholique) receive state funding under 1959 Debré law
Schools abroad for expatriate children follow different rules

laws.title: Immigration Law 2024
laws.subtitle: France's restrictive immigration reform amid political controversy
laws.fullDescription: France's 2024 Immigration Law (Loi Darmanin), passed with support from the far-right Rassemblement National, was one of the most restrictive immigration laws in French history: limiting family reunification, tightening welfare access for foreign nationals, imposing stricter language and civic knowledge requirements, and facilitating deportation. The Constitutional Council struck down some provisions. France processes 100,000+ asylum claims annually and has large North African immigrant communities. The debate reflects tension between France's laïcité tradition, labor needs, and political pressure from the far right.
laws.penalty: Irregular immigrants may be detained up to 90 days in retention centers (CRA) pending deportation; employing undocumented workers carries €15,000 fine per worker and potential imprisonment; visa overstays result in multi-year entry bans
exceptions: EU citizens have free movement rights and cannot be detained for immigration purposes
Unaccompanied minors cannot be detained in immigration detention

quiz.q: France's controversial 2024 immigration law was passed with the decisive votes of which political party?
quiz.explanation: The 2024 immigration law passed the French Senate with support from Marine Le Pen's Rassemblement National (National Rally), marking an unprecedented legislative partnership between the center-right government and the far-right that shocked many in French politics.

laws.title: Drug Law and Zero Tolerance Policy
laws.subtitle: France's strict drug laws amid Europe's highest cannabis use
laws.fullDescription: France has some of Europe's strictest drug laws but paradoxically the continent's highest cannabis usage rate. Simple drug use carries up to 1 year imprisonment and €3,750 fine — though in practice many receive civil fines (fixed penalty of €200 for cannabis use, implemented 2020). Drug trafficking carries 10 years (up to life for organized gangs). France has resisted drug liberalization despite EU neighbors' reforms. French police conduct regular stop-and-search operations in minority neighborhoods, creating documented racial bias in drug enforcement. France maintains a very restrictive approach to harm reduction.
laws.penalty: Drug use: up to 1 year jail/€3,750 fine OR €200 civil penalty; possession for personal use: same as use; trafficking: 10 years/€7.5 million fine; gang trafficking: up to life imprisonment; drug-related homicide: up to 30 years
exceptions: Medical cannabis pilot program approved 2021 and extended
Harm reduction services (needle exchanges, naloxone) funded by government
Minor offenders may receive treatment diversion
laws.sourceLabel: France Code de la santé publique – Drug Law

quiz.q: France has Europe's highest cannabis usage rate despite having strict drug laws. What civil penalty was introduced in 2020 for cannabis use?
quiz.explanation: France introduced a €200 fixed penalty notice (amende forfaitaire) for cannabis use in 2020, providing an alternative to the technically applicable 1-year imprisonment — a pragmatic approach to managing France's high cannabis usage without full legalization.

laws.title: Marriage for All (Mariage pour Tous)
laws.subtitle: France legalized same-sex marriage in 2013 amid large protests and celebrations
laws.fullDescription: France legalized same-sex marriage and adoption by same-sex couples on May 18, 2013, with the passage of the 'Marriage for All' law. The law was signed by President François Hollande after months of heated debate and large street protests both for and against. France also prohibits anti-LGBTQ+ discrimination and hate speech under the Penal Code. Same-sex couples have the same rights as heterosexual married couples.
laws.penalty: Anti-LGBTQ+ hate crimes carry enhanced penalties; discrimination is punishable by fines and imprisonment
exceptions: Individual religious ministers are not compelled to perform same-sex marriages

quiz.q: What was the popular name for France's same-sex marriage law passed in 2013?
quiz.explanation: The French law legalizing same-sex marriage was called 'Mariage pour Tous' (Marriage for All), signed into law by President Hollande in May 2013.

laws.title: Press Freedom With Strong Legal Protections
laws.subtitle: France has a long press freedom tradition anchored in the 1881 Press Law
laws.fullDescription: France's press freedom is protected by the 1789 Declaration of the Rights of Man and Citizen and the Republic's traditions. The Press Law of July 29, 1881, establishes the legal framework for media, including both protections and limits. France has strong source protection for journalists codified in law (Loi Dati 2010). France has a large media landscape including Le Monde, Le Figaro, Libération, and public broadcaster France Télévisions. France decriminalized defamation for matters of public interest. However, concentration of media ownership (particularly by billionaires like Bolloré) raises independence concerns.
laws.penalty: Press offenses are governed by the 1881 law with specific procedures; source protection is legally codified
exceptions: Denial of crimes against humanity and terrorism apology are criminalized

quiz.q: What landmark law governs press freedom and media regulation in France, still in effect today?
quiz.explanation: France's Press Law of July 29, 1881, is one of the oldest press freedom laws in the world, still governing the framework for media operations, press offenses, and protections — an extraordinary example of legal longevity.

laws.title: Avia Law and DSA Implementation — Online Hate Content
laws.subtitle: France aggressively implements EU digital laws and has its own anti-hate content legislation
laws.fullDescription: France passed the Avia Law (2020) requiring platforms to remove hate speech within one hour, but the Constitutional Council struck down key provisions as disproportionate. France then focused on implementing the EU Digital Services Act (DSA). France's ARCOM (digital regulatory authority) enforces content rules. France's CNIL (data protection authority) is one of the EU's most active GDPR enforcers, having fined Google (€150M), Facebook (€60M), and WhatsApp. The Loi SREN (2024) on digital space regulation adds further platform obligations. France is highly active in AI regulation discussions.
laws.penalty: CNIL GDPR fines in the hundreds of millions; ARCOM can impose DSA-related fines; SREN Act penalties
exceptions: Avia Law's most restrictive provisions were struck down; DSA framework applies instead

quiz.q: What happened to France's Avia Law provision requiring hate speech removal within one hour?
options: It was struck down by the Constitutional Council as disproportionate
It was expanded to cover misinformation
quiz.explanation: France's Avia Law provision requiring platforms to remove hate speech within one hour was struck down by France's Constitutional Council as disproportionate to free expression — pushing France to implement the more balanced EU Digital Services Act framework instead.

laws.title: Plan d'Épargne en Actions (PEA) Tax Advantage Rules
laws.subtitle: Strict compliance required for France's equity savings plan
laws.fullDescription: France's PEA allows residents to invest in European equities with significant tax advantages — after 5 years, capital gains and dividends are tax-free (though social charges apply). However, strict rules govern PEA accounts: only EU/EEA-listed shares qualify, annual deposits are capped at €150,000 (or €225,000 for PEA-PME), and early withdrawals before 5 years trigger full taxation plus penalties. The Autorité des marchés financiers (AMF) and Banque de France jointly regulate financial institutions offering PEA products.
laws.penalty: Early withdrawal triggers income tax plus 17.2% social charges on all gains; abusive use of PEA can result in account closure and full back-taxation
exceptions: Death of account holder triggers tax-free transfer
Disability and certain hardship cases allow early access without penalty
PEA-PME has separate higher cap for SME investments

quiz.q: What is the standard maximum deposit limit for a French PEA equity savings plan?
quiz.explanation: The standard PEA has a maximum deposit limit of €150,000. A separate PEA-PME for SME investments has a €225,000 cap.

laws.title: DGAL Food Safety & French Foodie Heritage Protection
laws.subtitle: France rigorously protects its culinary heritage through AOC/AOP designations
laws.fullDescription: France's Directorate General for Food (DGAL) under the Ministry of Agriculture oversees food safety for animal products, while DGCCRF (competition, consumer, and fraud authority) handles food fraud and labeling. France has one of the world's most elaborate systems of protected food designations: Appellation d'Origine Contrôlée (AOC) nationally and Appellation d'Origine Protégée (AOP) at EU level. These protect products like Champagne, Roquefort, Comté, Camembert de Normandie, and Bresse chicken — requiring production in specific regions using traditional methods. Food fraud against AOC/AOP designations is treated as criminal fraud. France's 'anti-waste' law (2020) requires supermarkets to donate unsold edible food.
laws.penalty: AOC/AOP fraud (selling non-qualifying product under protected name): criminal fraud charges, fines up to €300,000; food safety violations: DGAL can order recalls; anti-waste law violations: fines up to €3,750 per violation
exceptions: Home wine production for personal consumption under annual limits is permitted
Traditional 'fermier' (farm-gate) sales have modified hygiene requirements
Religious slaughter (shechita/halal) is permitted with specific authorization

quiz.q: What does France's 2020 anti-food-waste law require of supermarkets?
options: Charge for plastic bags on all food items
Donate all unsold but still edible food rather than disposing of it
Label all food with a countdown to expiration
Sell near-expiry food at 50% discount only
quiz.explanation: France's 2020 AGEC (anti-waste) law requires supermarkets to donate unsold but still edible food to food banks and charities rather than disposing of it — France was a pioneer globally in mandating food donation from retail.

laws.title: France Animal Sentience Recognition and Welfare Reform
laws.subtitle: France recognizes animals as sentient beings in Civil Code
laws.fullDescription: France made a landmark civil law reform in 2015, amending Article 515-14 of the Civil Code to explicitly recognize animals as 'sentient beings' (êtres vivants doués de sensibilité), removing them from the category of moveable property. The Penal Code Articles 521-1 to 521-2 criminalize acts of cruelty and serious abuse. France banned wild animals in circuses (effective 2028) and mink fur farming (effective 2025). The Loi Besson (1994) and subsequent reforms strengthened enforcement. France still has bullfighting in certain southern regions where it is classified as local cultural heritage (exception to animal cruelty laws). Foie gras remains contentious — it is legal and protected as 'cultural heritage'.
laws.penalty: Cruelty: up to 2 years and €30,000 fine; aggravated cruelty in groups or with death: 3 years and €45,000; animal sexual abuse: 2 years and €30,000
exceptions: Bullfighting in regions where it constitutes local cultural heritage
Foie gras production under heritage protection
Licensed hunting
Scientific research under ethics committee approval
laws.sourceLabel: Code Civil Art. 515-14 & Code Pénal Arts. 521-1

quiz.q: What significant legal change did France make to its Civil Code in 2015 regarding animals?
options: Animals were explicitly recognized as sentient beings, no longer classified as moveable property
All animals gained the right to legal representation
quiz.explanation: France's 2015 Civil Code amendment (Art. 515-14) explicitly defined animals as 'sentient living beings' — removing them from the category of moveable property and recognizing their capacity for suffering, a landmark step in French animal welfare law.

laws.title: France PACS and Divorce Law Reform
laws.subtitle: France's PACS civil partnership is widely used alternative to marriage
laws.fullDescription: French family law has two notable innovations. The Pacte Civil de Solidarité (PACS) — a civil partnership — was introduced in 1999 and has become enormously popular: by 2020, more PACS agreements were signed annually than marriages in France. PACS provides many marriage-like rights without full marriage, and is less complex to dissolve (simple declaration). France also reformed divorce law — since 2017, divorce by mutual consent (divorce par consentement mutuel) can be processed entirely by notary without any judge involvement when there are no disputes. France has a community of property (communauté réduite aux acquêts) as the default regime for married couples. France legalized same-sex marriage in 2013 (Mariage pour tous).
laws.penalty: Civil enforcement; pension alimentaire (support) enforced by huissier; criminal penalty for 'abandon de famille' — 2 years imprisonment and fines for persistent support non-payment
exceptions: Régime de séparation de biens (separation of property) by marital agreement
Pre-marital property retained
PACS dissolution simpler than divorce
laws.sourceLabel: French Civil Code — Droit de la Famille

quiz.q: What did France's 2017 divorce reform allow for uncontested divorces?
options: Notarial divorce — processing entirely by notary without any judge when there are no disputes
quiz.explanation: France's 2017 reform created 'divorce par consentement mutuel par acte sous signature privée contresigné par avocats' — allowing uncontested divorces to be processed entirely by a notary (with each spouse having their own lawyer) without any judicial involvement. This dramatically simplified and sped up uncontested divorces in France.

laws.title: France Loi Alur & Encadrement des Loyers
laws.subtitle: Rent control and social housing obligations
laws.fullDescription: France's property rights are governed by the Code Civil and major housing laws. The Loi ALUR (2014) introduced rent encadrement (controls) in 'zone tendue' (tight housing market) areas, limiting rents to 120% of local reference rents. The Loi SRU (2000) requires municipalities over 3,500 people to have 20-25% social housing (HLM) or face financial penalties. Landlords must provide a minimum 3-year lease (unfurnished) and cannot terminate without cause. The Loi Nogal (2021) strengthened tenant protections against evictions during winter months (treve hivernale, November-March).
laws.penalty: Illegal excess rent: tenant can demand repayment; SRU violations: municipal fine up to EUR 300 per missing social home per year
exceptions: Treve hivernale protects against evictions Nov-March
Furnished leases have minimum 1-year term
laws.source: Code Civil; Loi ALUR 2014; Loi SRU 2000

quiz.q: What does France's Loi SRU (2000) require from large municipalities?
options: 20-25% social housing stock or financial penalties
quiz.explanation: The Loi SRU (Solidarite et Renouvellement Urbains, 2000) requires municipalities over 3,500 people to maintain 20-25% social housing (HLM) or pay financial penalties, combating residential segregation.

laws.title: France Code de la Consommation & DGCCRF
laws.subtitle: Comprehensive consumer code and active enforcement
laws.fullDescription: France's Code de la Consommation consolidates consumer law including mandatory warranty (garantie legale de conformite, 2 years), 14-day withdrawal right for distance purchases (droit de retractation), and prohibition of abusive contract clauses (clauses abusives). The DGCCRF (Direction Generale de la Concurrence, de la Consommation et de la Repression des Fraudes) enforces consumer law with powers to issue injunctions and fines. Consumer associations (UFC-Que Choisir, 60 Millions de Consommateurs) are powerful and can file class actions since 2014 (action de groupe). France leads EU consumer protection lobbying and implemented the EU Omnibus Directive on fake reviews and price reduction transparency.
laws.penalty: 2-year garantie legale: repair or replace then partial refund; abusive clauses: void; DGCCRF fine up to EUR 300,000
exceptions: Action de groupe (class actions) available since 2014
EU Omnibus Directive implemented in France 2022
laws.source: Code de la Consommation; Loi Hamon 2014
laws.sourceLabel: France Code de la Consommation & DGCCRF

quiz.q: What is the French term for the mandatory legal warranty that applies to consumer goods purchases?
quiz.explanation: The garantie legale de conformite (legal conformity guarantee) is France's mandatory 2-year warranty on consumer goods — during which the seller must repair, replace, or refund defective items, with the burden of proof reversed in the consumer's favor for the first 12 months.

laws.title: Constitution de la Ve République — French Fifth Republic Constitution
laws.subtitle: France's 1958 Constitution establishing strong executive presidency
laws.fullDescription: France's current constitution (1958) established the Fifth Republic with a powerful executive president — a hybrid presidential-parliamentary system designed by de Gaulle to overcome parliamentary instability of the Fourth Republic. The Constitutional Council (Conseil Constitutionnel) reviews laws before promulgation (unlike Germany's reactive constitutional court). The 1958 Constitution has been amended 24+ times, notably adding the right to a healthy environment (2005). France's republican values include laïcité (secularism), and the Declaration of the Rights of Man (1789) is incorporated by reference. Emergency powers under Article 16 concentrate vast power in the President.
laws.penalty: Constitutional violations: Constitutional Council can strike down laws before promulgation. After 2010 QPC reform, courts can refer laws to Constitutional Council during cases.
exceptions: President has personal immunity from prosecution while in office (Constitutional Council ruling)
Emergency constitutional provisions under Article 16 have few procedural checks
Organic laws require mandatory Constitutional Council review

quiz.q: Why did de Gaulle design France's Fifth Republic constitution with such strong presidential powers?
options: To overcome the chronic governmental instability of the Fourth Republic
To comply with NATO membership requirements
To integrate the French empire into the republic
quiz.explanation: The Fourth Republic (1946-1958) was characterized by extreme parliamentary instability — 21 governments in 12 years. De Gaulle designed the Fifth Republic's constitution to create strong executive leadership, particularly through the directly elected presidency, reducing parliament's power to bring down governments.

laws.title: CNIL — Commission Nationale de l'Informatique et des Libertés
laws.subtitle: France's powerful data protection authority — among EU's most active GDPR enforcers
laws.fullDescription: France's CNIL (National Commission for Computing and Freedoms), established 1978 — before the internet — is one of the world's oldest and most powerful data protection authorities. CNIL enforces the EU GDPR plus France's own data protection law (Loi Informatique et Libertés). CNIL has issued major GDPR fines: €150 million against Google (2022), €150 million against Facebook (2022), €60 million against Microsoft (2022) for cookie consent violations. CNIL also has broader powers: it can regulate algorithmic decision-making, AI systems, and has issued guidance on facial recognition and AI in education. France was an early pioneer in recognizing 'le droit à l'oubli' (right to be forgotten) in 1970s.
laws.penalty: GDPR violations: up to €20M or 4% global turnover. CNIL can order immediate data processing suspension. Public reprimands are common.
exceptions: Public authorities processing for security purposes have special rules
Research and public health processing has derogations
Journalistic processing of public figures has wider latitude
laws.sourceLabel: CNIL — Commission Nationale de l'Informatique et des Libertés

quiz.q: When was France's CNIL data protection authority established?
quiz.explanation: France's CNIL was established in 1978 by the Loi Informatique et Libertés — one of the world's first national data protection authorities, predating the internet age. This early establishment reflects France's strong philosophical tradition of privacy rights dating to the Enlightenment.

laws.title: Code du Travail — 35-Hour Work Week
laws.subtitle: France's famous legal work time limits and labor code
laws.fullDescription: France's Code du Travail (Labor Code) establishes the famous 35-hour legal work week (introduced 2000 under Jospin government). Working beyond 35 hours requires overtime pay at 125% (first 8 hours) and 150% (additional hours). However, many companies use forfait-jours (day-based contracts) for executives that effectively bypass hourly limits. The French Labor Code is extremely comprehensive — over 3,500 pages. Dismissals require serious/real cause and formal procedure; wrongful dismissal is expensive. CDI (permanent contracts) are preferred; CDD (fixed-term) are strictly limited. The 2017 Macron Ordinances significantly liberalized some provisions through collective bargaining.
laws.penalty: Unauthorized overtime: fines, labor court orders. Unfair dismissal: reinstatement or damages (capped by Macron scale — challenged by courts).
exceptions: Executive managers on forfait-jours are exempt from hourly tracking
Certain sectors (healthcare, transport) have sector-specific agreements
Annualization agreements allow weekly variation within annual total

quiz.q: What is France's legal maximum work week under the Code du Travail?
quiz.explanation: France established a 35-hour legal work week in 2000 (Aubry Laws). Hours beyond 35 require overtime pay. However, many professionals are on 'forfait-jours' contracts counted in days rather than hours, effectively exempting them from the 35-hour cap while maintaining annual leave protections.

laws.title: Laïcité à l'École — Secularism in French Public Schools
laws.subtitle: France's strict secularism laws banning religious symbols in public schools
laws.fullDescription: France's laïcité (secularism) is a constitutional principle with a unique intensity. The 2004 law bans 'conspicuous religious symbols' in public primary and secondary schools — specifically interpreted to prohibit headscarves (hijab), kippot, large crosses, turbans, and other visible religious symbols worn by students. The law was primarily aimed at the headscarf but is religion-neutral in text. Public school teachers cannot wear religious symbols. In 2023, abayas (full-length robes) were banned from schools as violating laïcité. France has about 5 million Muslim citizens (largest Muslim minority in EU) and the headscarf ban has been highly controversial internationally.
laws.penalty: Students wearing banned symbols: sent home, parents contacted. Persistent non-compliance: suspension or transfer to private religious school.
exceptions: Private religious schools (écoles sous contrat) are not subject to the ban
Universities (higher education) are NOT subject to the 2004 law
Religious instruction in Alsace-Moselle (historical exception) continues
laws.sourceLabel: Loi 2004-228 — Signes religieux dans les écoles

quiz.q: In which educational institutions does France's 2004 ban on religious symbols apply?
options: Public primary and secondary schools only
quiz.explanation: France's 2004 law on religious symbols applies specifically to public primary and secondary schools (enseignement primaire et secondaire), not universities. The Constitutional Council ruled that university students retain freedom of religion as adults, making university campuses outside the scope of the 2004 law.

laws.title: Loi Sapin II — French Anti-Corruption Law
laws.subtitle: France's major anti-corruption framework with AFA and whistleblower protections
laws.fullDescription: France's Loi Sapin II (2016) was a landmark anti-corruption reform. It established the AFA (Agence Française Anticorruption), required large companies (500+ employees, €100M+ turnover) to implement anti-corruption compliance programs, created a whistleblower protection framework, and criminalized 'influence peddling' more broadly. It also created the Convention Judiciaire d'Intérêt Public (CJIP) — a French version of a deferred prosecution agreement allowing companies to settle without criminal conviction. The Sapin II framework was a major step for France, which had been criticized for weak anti-corruption enforcement. The 2022 Loi pour la confiance dans l'institution judiciaire strengthened whistleblower protections.
laws.penalty: AFA non-compliance: fines up to €200,000 (natural person) or €1M (legal person). Corruption: up to 10 years imprisonment, €1M fine.
exceptions: SMEs under thresholds have simplified compliance requirements
Public officials have separate disciplinary procedures
Diplomatic immunity applies to certain foreign officials

quiz.q: What new prosecutorial tool did Loi Sapin II introduce in France, similar to US deferred prosecution agreements?
quiz.explanation: Loi Sapin II created the Convention Judiciaire d'Intérêt Public (CJIP), allowing the Parquet National Financier (financial prosecutor) to reach agreements with companies accused of corruption, laundering, or tax fraud without criminal conviction, in exchange for fines, compliance programs, and compensation to the state.

laws.title: Sécurité Sociale — French Universal Health Coverage
laws.subtitle: France's nationally-ranked healthcare system and assurance maladie
laws.fullDescription: France's Sécurité Sociale provides near-universal health coverage through the Assurance Maladie (Health Insurance). France consistently ranks at or near the top of global healthcare rankings. The 'remboursement' system allows patients to see any doctor and receive reimbursement of 70-100% depending on treatment and physician type. Mutuelles (supplemental insurance) cover most remaining costs. France has a '100% Santé' program providing full coverage for basic dental, optical, and hearing aids. The carte Vitale (green electronic health card) simplifies claims. France spends about 12% of GDP on health (one of Europe's highest). Primary care gatekeeper reform has increased care coordination.
laws.penalty: Employers must register all employees for social security. Non-declaration: criminal fines, back contributions. Social security fraud: repayment plus penalties.
exceptions: Expats and self-employed have separate contribution schemes
PUMA (Protection Universelle Maladie) covers those without employment-based access
Emergency care provided regardless of insurance status

quiz.q: What does France's '100% Santé' program provide?
options: Full coverage for all medical treatments
Full coverage for basic dental, optical, and hearing aids
quiz.explanation: France's 100% Santé program (launched 2019-2021) ensures that for basic dental care (bridges, crowns), optical (glasses), and hearing aids, patients can choose options with zero out-of-pocket costs — covered 100% by Assurance Maladie and mutuelles. This addressed a major gap where many French people avoided these treatments due to cost.

laws.title: Loi Climat et Résilience — Climate and Resilience Law
laws.subtitle: France's 2021 comprehensive climate law from Citizens' Climate Convention
laws.fullDescription: France's Loi Climat et Résilience (2021) implemented recommendations from the Citizens' Climate Convention (CCC) — 150 randomly selected citizens who proposed over 140 measures. The law covers: transport (banning flights where train alternative under 2.5 hours exists), buildings (banning new gas boilers, thermal renovation obligations for energy-intensive housing), advertising (banning ads for high-carbon products), agriculture, and consumption. France targets carbon neutrality by 2050. The Climate and Energy Agency (ADEME) coordinates implementation. France has a constitutional commitment to protecting the environment (2005 Charter for the Environment). Critics said CCC recommendations were watered down.
laws.penalty: Building energy renovation: landlords cannot raise rents on thermal 'sieves' (lowest energy ratings). Gas boiler ban in new buildings from 2022.
exceptions: Heritage buildings have modified thermal renovation requirements
Rural areas have more flexibility on short-haul flight bans
Agricultural emissions handled through separate CAP framework

quiz.q: What unique democratic process produced the recommendations for France's 2021 climate law?
options: A Citizens' Climate Convention of 150 randomly selected citizens
quiz.explanation: France's Citizens' Climate Convention (Convention Citoyenne pour le Climat) — 150 citizens randomly selected to represent French society — spent 9 months producing 146 recommendations. President Macron committed to implementing them 'without filter,' though critics said significant weakening occurred in the resulting law.

laws.title: Loi Renseignement — Intelligence and Surveillance Law
laws.subtitle: France's intelligence legislation expanded after terrorist attacks
laws.fullDescription: Following the 2015 Paris attacks (Charlie Hebdo and Bataclan), France significantly expanded intelligence powers through the Loi Renseignement (2015). The law legalized bulk metadata collection, algorithm-based surveillance for threat detection, international cable interception, and IMSI catchers. A new Conseil National du Renseignement oversees six intelligence services. Post-2015, France maintained a state of emergency for nearly 2 years — many emergency provisions were subsequently incorporated into ordinary law (2017 Loi Renforçant la Sécurité Intérieure). The Charlie Hebdo and Bataclan attacks killed 130+ people and transformed French security policy. Annual terrorism prosecutions have increased significantly.
laws.penalty: Terrorism: up to 20 years (life for leaders). CSIRT data retention requirements for operators. Judges can authorize 'black box' algorithmic surveillance.
exceptions: Parliamentary delegation (DNLF) reviews intelligence activities
CNCTR (oversight body) gives prior authorization for most surveillance
Journalistic sources have some protection from intelligence gathering

quiz.q: What major event prompted France to significantly expand surveillance powers through the 2015 Loi Renseignement?
options: The 2015 Charlie Hebdo and Paris attacks
quiz.explanation: The January 2015 Charlie Hebdo massacre and November 2015 Paris attacks (Bataclan concert hall and cafés, killing 130 people) led France to pass the Loi Renseignement in July 2015, significantly expanding intelligence gathering powers including bulk metadata collection and algorithmic surveillance.

laws.title: Loi Evin — French Alcohol and Tobacco Advertising Restrictions
laws.subtitle: France's strict rules limiting alcohol advertising and tobacco promotion
laws.fullDescription: France's Loi Évin (1991) severely restricts alcohol and tobacco advertising. Tobacco advertising is essentially banned entirely. Alcohol advertising is limited to specific authorized channels (press targeting adults, radio with time restrictions, billboards in limited contexts) with mandatory health warnings. No alcohol advertising is permitted during events primarily attracting youth. The law has been contested by alcohol producers and sporting event organizers. During major sporting events, France's laws have conflicted with international sponsor visibility requirements. The Loi Évin also prohibits smoking in workplaces and public places (partially predating the 2007 comprehensive ban). France has one of Europe's highest tobacco tax rates.
laws.penalty: Illegal tobacco advertising: criminal fines. Alcohol advertising violations: fines up to €75,000, confiscation of ads.
exceptions: Wine and spirits regions can use geographical indications in certain promotional contexts
Press articles about alcohol (not advertising) are permitted
Tasting events in designated premises are not advertising

quiz.q: What is unique about France's Loi Évin during international sporting events?
options: France bans all foreign sports sponsorship
French law restricts alcohol sponsor visibility, conflicting with international sports organization requirements
Stadium alcohol sales are banned during events
quiz.explanation: France's Loi Évin creates conflicts during major events like the Tour de France or Euro football championships, where international sports bodies require alcohol brand visibility in stadiums and broadcasts. France has negotiated exemptions for some events while maintaining its general advertising restrictions.

laws.title: Droit d'Asile — French Asylum and Immigration Law
laws.subtitle: France's asylum process and controversial immigration reform debates
laws.fullDescription: France receives among the EU's highest asylum applications (100,000+ annually). The OFPRA (Office for Protection of Refugees and Stateless Persons) processes asylum claims; appeals go to CNDA (National Court for Right of Asylum). Status determination averages 5-6 months. France has strong constitutional protection of the right to asylum (1946 Constitution preamble). President Macron's 2023 immigration law (Loi Immigration) was among France's most contested — the Constitutional Council struck down significant portions. France also enforces Operation Néo for sea rescues and has tensions with the UK over Channel crossings. The French republican model emphasizes assimilation (intégration républicaine) over multiculturalism.
laws.penalty: Illegal entry: up to 1 year imprisonment, deportation. Document fraud: up to 5 years. Employing undocumented workers: fines of €15,000 per worker.
exceptions: Unaccompanied minors have special protection regardless of entry method
European Convention on Human Rights prevents deportation to torture/persecution
Family reunification rights are constitutionally protected

quiz.q: Which body hears appeals against OFPRA asylum rejections in France?
options: The CNDA (National Court for Right of Asylum)
quiz.explanation: Asylum seekers whose claims are rejected by OFPRA can appeal to the CNDA (Cour Nationale du Droit d'Asile — National Court for Right of Asylum), a specialized administrative court. Further appeals on points of law go to the Conseil d'État.

laws.title: AMF — Autorité des Marchés Financiers
laws.subtitle: France's securities and financial markets regulator
laws.fullDescription: France's AMF (Financial Markets Authority) regulates securities markets, investment funds, and financial intermediaries. France is home to the Paris stock exchange (Euronext Paris), luxury conglomerates (LVMH, Hermès) and major banks (BNP Paribas, Société Générale). The AMF enforces insider trading rules, market manipulation prohibitions, and collective investment regulations. France's financial sector was heavily involved in the 2008 crisis (Société Générale's 'rogue trader' Jérôme Kerviel lost €4.9 billion in 2007-2008). France has been aggressive in attracting financial firms post-Brexit, with many moving European operations from London to Paris. The ACPR supervises banking and insurance.
laws.penalty: Insider trading: up to 10 years imprisonment, €100M fine (or 10x profit). Market manipulation: similar penalties. AMF administrative sanctions up to €100M.
exceptions: Market makers have exemptions from some market manipulation rules
Buyback programs following notification are exempt from price manipulation rules
Central bank operations are exempt

quiz.q: What famous French bank case became a global reference for rogue trading risk?
quiz.explanation: Jérôme Kerviel, a trader at Société Générale, accumulated unauthorized positions totaling €50 billion in 2007-2008. When discovered, unwinding the positions caused losses of €4.9 billion — the largest rogue trading loss in history at the time. Kerviel was convicted of fraud and breach of trust.

laws.title: Loi ALUR — Housing Access and Urban Renovation Law
laws.subtitle: France's rent control and tenant protection framework in tight markets
laws.fullDescription: France's Loi ALUR (2014) and subsequent reforms established rent control (encadrement des loyers) in tense housing markets like Paris and Lyon. Rent cannot exceed a reference rent + 20% cap. Paris implemented encadrement in 2019 after an earlier attempt was ruled illegal. France has the Droit au Logement Opposable (DALO) — a legally enforceable right to housing, allowing homeless individuals to sue the state if not housed. The 'trêve hivernale' (winter truce) bans evictions from November 1 to March 31. France has significant social housing (HLM — habitations à loyer modéré) — about 17% of housing stock. Long eviction procedures (12-18+ months) create a 'culture of non-payment' risk.
laws.penalty: Exceeding rent cap: tenant can demand rent reduction and repayment of excess. Illegal evictions: criminal prosecution. Trêve hivernale violations: serious criminal exposure.
exceptions: New construction and heavily renovated properties temporarily exempt from rent caps
Rural areas outside designated tense zones not subject to caps
Student and seasonal accommodation have separate rules

quiz.q: What is the 'trêve hivernale' in French housing law?
options: A summer vacation period when courts don't process housing cases
A winter ban on tenant evictions from November 1 to March 31
A freeze on rent increases during winter months
A moratorium on foreclosures during economic downturns
quiz.explanation: The trêve hivernale (winter truce) is a French law provision that prohibits the eviction of tenants between November 1 and March 31, regardless of the reason for eviction. The rationale is protection from homelessness during the coldest months. Utility disconnections are also suspended during this period for non-payment.

laws.title: SNCF et Droit de Grève — Railway Strikes and Service Continuity
laws.subtitle: France's controversial union strike rights vs. minimum service guarantees
laws.fullDescription: France has among the world's highest strike rates in public transport, especially railways (SNCF) and Paris Metro (RATP). After major disruptions, France's 2007 Loi sur le Dialogue Social et la Continuité du Service Public introduced minimum service requirements: workers must declare strike intent 48 hours in advance, companies must inform users 24 hours before disruption, and minimum service levels must be maintained. However, SNCF and RATP strikes remain frequent and disruptive. The 2018 SNCF reform (cheminot special status for new hires abolished) triggered months-long rolling strikes. French labor unions (CGT, FO, CFDT, UNSA) are legally powerful but have relatively low membership rates.
laws.penalty: Companies not maintaining minimum service: administrative fines. Union illegal wildcats: labor court action, potential damages.
exceptions: Some essential services (police, hospitals) have more restrictive strike rules
Right to strike is constitutionally protected
EU services have freedom of movement protections overriding some strikes

quiz.q: Under France's 2007 law on public service strikes, how much notice must striking workers give?
quiz.explanation: France's 2007 law requires transport workers intending to strike to declare their intention 48 hours in advance. This allows companies to inform users 24 hours before disruptions begin. However, this only applies to the first strike declaration — successive strike days don't require repeated 48-hour notices.

laws.title: Code Pénal — Prohibition of Denial of Recognized Genocides
laws.subtitle: France's Gayssot Act criminalizing Holocaust denial and genocide denial
laws.fullDescription: France's Loi Gayssot (1990) criminalizes contesting the existence of crimes against humanity as defined by the Nuremberg Tribunal — effectively criminalizing Holocaust denial. Subsequently, France passed the Loi Taubira (2001) recognizing the slave trade and slavery as crimes against humanity, and the 2011 law recognizing the Armenian Genocide and criminalizing its denial — though the latter was struck down by the Constitutional Council and a revised version was again struck down in 2012. France's hate speech laws are among Europe's most extensive, covering press law and the Code Pénal. Online hate speech has triggered major platform fines under France's Avia law (partially struck down).
laws.penalty: Holocaust denial: up to 1 year imprisonment, €45,000 fine under Gayssot. Hate speech in press: up to 1 year, €45,000. Racist insults: up to 6 months, €22,500.
exceptions: Academic historical research and debate is protected
Journalism and commentary on historical events is permitted
Criticism of religions, ideologies, and practices is distinguishable from prohibited hatred

quiz.q: Why was France's 2011 law criminalizing denial of the Armenian Genocide struck down by the Constitutional Council?
options: The Armenian Genocide was not legally recognized by France
The law violated freedom of speech/research without sufficient justification in law
France has no jurisdiction over foreign genocides
The law conflicted with EU free movement law
quiz.explanation: The Constitutional Council struck down the 2011 law criminalizing Armenian Genocide denial, ruling it violated freedom of expression and communication. The Council distinguished it from the Gayssot law (which covers crimes defined by a French/international judicial body) — the Armenian Genocide, while recognized by France, was not defined by such a tribunal.

laws.title: DGSI / DGSE — French Internal and External Intelligence Services
laws.subtitle: France's dual domestic and foreign intelligence services framework
laws.fullDescription: France's internal intelligence is DGSI (Directorate-General for Internal Security, formerly DST/RG), while external intelligence is DGSE (similar to MI6 or CIA). Both operate under the 2015 Intelligence Law after the post-Charlie Hebdo reforms. France has six intelligence services total. The CNRLT (National Counter-Terrorism Prosecutor) handles terrorism prosecutions with specially designated judges (juges d'instruction). France has a tradition of the 'juge d'instruction' (investigating magistrate) for serious crimes — though being reformed. Political intelligence scandals have periodically emerged (Elf Aquitaine, Rainbow Warrior). France conducts extensive signals intelligence (SIGINT) as a nuclear power and permanent UN Security Council member.
laws.penalty: Intelligence laws apply to surveillance authorization; violations by agents face prosecution. Unauthorized intelligence disclosure: up to 7 years imprisonment.
exceptions: Parliamentary intelligence delegation (DGSNR) oversight
CNCTR provides prior authorization for most surveillance
Sources protection for journalists recognized but not absolute
laws.sourceLabel: SGDSN — Secrétariat Général de la Défense et de la Sécurité Nationale

quiz.q: What type of French legal official has historically played a central role in major criminal and terrorism investigations?
quiz.explanation: The juge d'instruction (investigating magistrate) is a uniquely French legal institution — an independent judge who conducts in-depth criminal investigations with powers to order searches, wiretaps, arrests, and question witnesses. Major cases like the Clearstream affair, Elf Aquitaine scandal, and most terrorism cases have been handled by these juges d'instruction.

laws.title: Loi sur les Nouvelles Régulations Économiques — Corporate Governance
laws.subtitle: France's corporate governance requirements for listed companies
laws.fullDescription: France's company law (Code de Commerce) and successive corporate governance reforms require listed companies to have independent directors, separate audit committees, and pay disclosure (say-on-pay votes). The 'Loi Pacte' (2019) introduced major corporate law changes: simplified business creation, employee shareholding requirements, and created the concept of 'société à mission' (purpose-driven company) — similar to US benefit corporations. French law traditionally gives considerable power to major shareholders (actionnaires de référence) in dual-class share structures. The French state remains a major shareholder in 'national champions' including EDF, Air France, and Renault.
laws.penalty: Corporate governance violations by listed companies: AMF sanctions, shareholder litigation. Board decisions without required oversight: potentially voidable.
exceptions: Société à mission status requires purpose inscription but is voluntary
Employee director requirements apply from 1,000+ employees
State-owned enterprises have additional governance requirements

quiz.q: What new legal company form did France's Loi Pacte (2019) create, similar to a US benefit corporation?
quiz.explanation: France's Loi Pacte introduced the 'société à mission' (purpose-driven company), allowing businesses to inscribe social and environmental objectives in their statutes alongside profit. This is similar to the US PBC (Public Benefit Corporation). Notable examples include Danone, which adopted this status in 2020 before activist investors forced changes to its leadership.

laws.title: PACS — Civil Solidarity Pact
laws.subtitle: France's civil partnership law predating and complementing same-sex marriage
laws.fullDescription: France's PACS (Pacte Civil de Solidarité), enacted 1999, created a civil partnership available to same-sex and different-sex couples. Initially controversial, it became very popular — more PACSes are registered annually than marriages in France. PACS provides tax benefits, inheritance rights, and mutual support obligations, but fewer rights than marriage (particularly regarding children and international recognition). France legalized same-sex marriage in 2013 (Mariage pour Tous) over significant controversy. PACS remains popular as a lighter commitment that can be dissolved more easily than marriage. France provides equal parental rights regardless of marital status — the Autorité Parentale applies equally to unmarried parents.
laws.penalty: False declaration for PACS (e.g., for residency/tax advantages): criminal fraud, annulment of PACS.
exceptions: PACS between close relatives or existing marriage holders is prohibited
Foreign nationals' PACS may not be recognized in their home country
International recognition of PACS for immigration varies by country

quiz.q: Why did PACS become more popular than marriage in France, despite originally being designed for same-sex couples?
options: Tax benefits are greater under PACS than marriage
PACS is simpler to dissolve than marriage — no divorce proceedings required
Religious institutions endorsed PACS over civil marriage
quiz.explanation: PACS can be dissolved by simple registered letter to the civil registry, without the complex divorce proceedings required to end a marriage. This flexibility, combined with substantial tax and legal benefits, made PACS attractive to both same-sex and different-sex couples as an alternative to marriage.

laws.title: Code de Procédure Pénale — Rights in Garde à Vue (Police Custody)
laws.subtitle: French criminal procedure rights including custody notification and legal access
laws.fullDescription: French criminal procedure (Code de Procédure Pénale) was significantly reformed in 2011 to comply with European Convention on Human Rights. A person placed in garde à vue (police custody) must now be: immediately informed of their rights, allowed to contact a family member/employer, provided with a medical examination, and crucially — given access to a lawyer from the start of custody. Before 2011, lawyer access was only after 24 hours. Custody can last 24 hours, extendable to 48 hours with prosecutor authorization, and up to 96 hours for terrorism. The Constitutional Council has been activist in striking down criminal procedure violations. Preventive detention (détention provisoire) requires judicial authorization.
laws.penalty: Custody without informing of rights: evidence potentially inadmissible. Illegal search: evidence exclusion. Extended custody without authorization: criminal liability for officers.
exceptions: Terrorism cases have extended custody periods
Organized crime cases have modified access rules
Emergency situations may delay but not eliminate notification requirements

quiz.q: What major reform to French garde à vue (police custody) was made in 2011?
options: Required recording of all police interviews
Gave access to a lawyer from the start of custody (previously after 24 hours)
Required judicial authorization for all custody
quiz.explanation: Following European Court of Human Rights rulings, France's 2011 reform gave suspects access to a lawyer from the very beginning of garde à vue. Previously, under French inquisitorial tradition, lawyer access was only after 20-24 hours. The reform was prompted by multiple ECtHR judgments against France.

laws.title: AOC/AOP — French Agricultural Origin Protection Law
laws.subtitle: France's appellations d'origine — protecting regional wine, cheese, and food names
laws.fullDescription: France's system of Appellations d'Origine Contrôlée/Protégée (AOC/AOP) is a legal framework protecting geographical indication of origin for wines, cheeses, and agricultural products. Using 'Champagne' for non-Champagne-region sparkling wine, 'Bordeaux' for non-Bordeaux wine, or 'Roquefort' for non-AOC sheep's milk blue cheese is illegal in France and EU countries. INAO (Institut National de l'Origine et de la Qualité) oversees AOC/AOP certifications. France has 400+ food AOPs and 400+ wine AOCs. The system was the model for the EU's Protected Designation of Origin (PDO) regulation. France aggressively litigates globally to protect its appellations — ongoing disputes with US, Australia, and others.
laws.penalty: Misuse of protected name in EU: administrative fines, injunctions, product confiscation. Criminal prosecution possible for systematic fraud.
exceptions: Generic use of terms before AOC existed may have grandfather rights in some markets
Non-EU countries negotiate trademark recognition separately
Research and educational use of protected names is permitted
laws.sourceLabel: INAO — Institut National de l'Origine et de la Qualité

quiz.q: What is the global significance of France's AOC system?
options: First country to tax alcohol by regional origin
Model for the EU's entire Protected Designation of Origin (PDO) regulation
First country to ban foreign wine imports
Basis for international wine labeling standards
quiz.explanation: France's Appellation d'Origine Contrôlée (AOC) system, developed from the 1919 wine appellation laws, became the direct model for the EU's Protected Designation of Origin (PDO/AOP) regulation. The principle that geographic origin confers specific quality characteristics and deserves legal protection is now embedded in EU and international trade law.

laws.title: Loi Toubon — French Language Protection Law
laws.subtitle: France's law mandating French in commercial and public communications
laws.fullDescription: France's Loi Toubon (1994) requires the use of French language in: advertising, consumer contracts, job descriptions, instructions/manuals, and public service communications in France. The Académie française (founded 1635) advises on French language purity and neologisms. DGLFLF (Délégation Générale à la Langue Française et aux Langues de France) promotes French. The law was partly struck down by the Constitutional Council regarding private individuals. France has a deep political commitment to defending the French language domestically and internationally (Organisation Internationale de la Francophonie). International academic conferences in France may still be conducted in English despite the law.
laws.penalty: Advertising violations: fines up to €750. Consumer contract violations: null provisions replaced by French law equivalents. Systematic violations: up to €37,500.
exceptions: Communications specifically targeting foreign audiences are exempt
Academic publications in international scientific journals exempt
Radio/TV quotas for French music apply separately

quiz.q: What institution, founded by Cardinal Richelieu in 1635, officially regulates the French language?
quiz.explanation: The Académie française, founded in 1635, is the official guardian of the French language. Its 40 'immortal' members produce the official dictionary of French and recommend French equivalents for foreign words (e.g., 'courriel' for email, 'nuage' for cloud computing). However, its recommendations are advisory, not legally binding.
